case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a generic drug manufacturer can be held liable for inducement of infringement of a brand’s method-of-use patents based on the generic’s marketing and labeling practices—despite a “skinny label” carve-out—when the complaint pleads a fact-specific set of circumstances suggesting the generic encouraged patented uses.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) (induced infringement), in the background of the Hatch-Waxman Act framework for abbreviated new drug applications (21 U.S.C. § 355(j)) and associated “carve-out/skinny label” practices.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Hikma) argue that the Federal Circuit improperly allowed an inducement claim to proceed on allegations that are consistent with lawful generic competition under Hatch-Waxman, particularly where the generic used a skinny label intended to avoid patented indications. They contend inducement under § 271(b) requires well-pleaded facts showing specific intent to encourage infringement and affirmative acts directed to the patented method, not merely (i) foreseeable off-label prescribing, (ii) residual references or market realities, or (iii) ordinary steps taken to sell an FDA-approved generic. Petitioners warn the decision undermines Congress’s skinny-label pathway, chills generic entry, and effectively converts method-of-use patents into broader barriers than the statute permits.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Amarin) argue that, given the ‘particular constellation of facts’ alleged, they plausibly pleaded active inducement: that Hikma took affirmative steps—through its labeling/communications/marketing context and how the product was positioned in the marketplace—to encourage physicians and others to use the generic for Amarin’s patented methods, even if the generic nominally carved out the patented indication. They emphasize that inducement is a fact-intensive inquiry and that at the pleading stage the complaint need only make it plausible that Hikma intended to cause the patented use and took actions that in context promoted that use, rather than merely selling a product capable of both infringing and non-infringing uses.
key_precedents: Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. (2011) (knowledge/intent standards for inducement)
DSU Medical Corp. v. JMS Co. (Fed. Cir.) (specific intent requirement for § 271(b) inducement)
MGM Studios Inc. v. Grokster, Ltd. (2005) (inducement principles by analogy, often cited in patent inducement discussions)
Warner-Lambert Co. v. Apotex Corp. (Fed. Cir.) (inducement and method-of-use claims involving pharmaceuticals)
AstraZeneca LP v. Apotex, Inc. (Fed. Cir.) (skinny label and inducement in pharmaceutical context)
GlaxoSmithKline LLC v. Teva Pharmaceuticals USA, Inc. (Fed. Cir.) (inducement liability and skinny label issues; fact-specific approach)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right that Grokster permits intent to be inferred from a pattern of “expression and conduct,” and that a skinny label is not categorical immunity. But their “constellation” framing, as applied here, does not plausibly allege the Global-Tech/Commil requirement of affirmative steps purposefully aimed at bringing about the patented method; the pleaded facts remain at least as consistent with FDA-compliant participation in Congress’s § viii carve-out plus foreseeable off-label use as with culpable encouragement. Justice Jackson’s fairness concern about discovery is real, yet Rule 12 still demands a plausible inference of specific intent, and we should not dilute § 271(b)’s “actively induces” into foreseeability-plus in a way that would destabilize Hatch-Waxman’s reliance interests. A narrow disposition—dismissal on these pleadings while expressly reserving liability where targeted promotion or directed communications are plausibly alleged—best preserves both inducement doctrine and the statutory scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor rightly emphasize that intent may be proven circumstantially and that a skinny label is not categorical immunity, and Grokster permits inference from “expression and conduct.” But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, their “constellation” theory—on these pleadings—rests on facts equally consistent with Congress’s § viii carve-out and lawful, FDA-compliant sales in a market where off-label use is common, which cannot plausibly establish the specific, purposeful encouragement that § 271(b)’s text (“actively induces”) requires under Global-Tech and Commil. Under an originalist, textualist reading, “active inducement” demands pleaded facts showing affirmative steps directed to bring about the patented method, not foreseeability-plus derived from market realities. This leaves intact inducement liability where targeted promotion of the patented use is plausibly alleged, while preserving Hatch-Waxman’s structure against dilution by inference untethered to directed encouragement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right that intent can be inferred circumstantially and that a skinny label is not categorical immunity; Grokster permits inference from “expression and conduct.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, the complaint here still must plausibly allege “active” inducement under § 271(b)—affirmative steps purposefully directed to bring about the patented method—not a set of facts equally consistent with Congress’s § viii carve-out operating as intended in a mixed-use market. Justice Jackson’s fairness point about discovery does not justify relaxing the Rule 12 plausibility requirement in a way that effectively converts predictable off-label use into specific intent, which would dilute “actively induces” into foreseeability-plus contrary to Global-Tech and Commil. On these pleadings, absent particularized allegations of targeted communications or instructions steering prescribers to the patented use, dismissal best preserves Hatch-Waxman’s structure while leaving room for stronger inducement claims when truly directed promotion is alleged.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—that Global-Tech and Commil demand purposeful, culpable encouragement and that we must not let a “constellation” theory collapse § 271(b) into mere foreseeability in a § viii skinny-label world—has real force, especially to preserve Hatch-Waxman’s reliance interests. But Grokster also makes clear that intent may be inferred from “expression and conduct,” and requiring a near-explicit, targeted instruction at Rule 12 risks creating an extra-textual safe harbor keyed to FDA posture rather than to whether the defendant plausibly took affirmative steps to bring about the patented method. A skinny label is powerful evidence against intent, yet it cannot be categorical immunity where the complaint plausibly alleges additional acts and context-based messaging that steer prescribers toward the patented use; inducement is fact-intensive, and foreclosing discovery when intent is typically circumstantial would unduly burden enforcement of method patents. Properly applied, the pleading line should screen out “market realities alone” (as Justice Alito warns) while allowing claims that plausibly allege purposeful encouragement beyond lawful sales and foreseeable off-label use.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s best point is that a “constellation” theory can devolve into foreseeability-plus and thereby dilute § 271(b)’s “actively induces” into something close to lawful participation in a mixed-use market—an outcome Global-Tech and Commil do not permit. But I do not read our approach (as Justice Sotomayor frames it) to allow liability on market realities alone; Grokster expressly allows intent to be inferred from “expression and conduct,” and the question at Rule 12 is whether the pleaded affirmative acts and context plausibly support purposeful encouragement, not whether the complaint contains a single targeted instruction. Justice Kavanaugh’s proposed requirement of a “clear, directed communication” risks becoming an extra-textual safe harbor keyed to the presence of a skinny label rather than a textual inquiry into whether the defendant took affirmative steps intending to bring about the patented method. The administrable middle ground is to insist on nonconclusory allegations of affirmative, culpable encouragement beyond mere sale/foreseeability, while rejecting a heightened pleading rule that would categorically privilege § viii compliance over § 271(b)’s intent-focused standard.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right that Grokster allows intent to be inferred circumstantially and that a § viii carve-out is not categorical immunity, but their “constellation” theory still must satisfy the statutory demand that one “actively induces” infringement, as Global-Tech and Commil require—purposeful, culpable encouragement, not merely predictable off-label use in a mixed market. Justice Jackson’s fairness concern about discovery has force, yet Rule 12 still requires nonconclusory facts making specific intent plausible, and allegations equally consistent with FDA-compliant participation in Hatch-Waxman’s carve-out do not plausibly show the requisite affirmative, directed encouragement. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, diluting “actively” into foreseeability-plus would effectively penalize Congress’s authorized skinny-label pathway; on these pleadings I do not see pleaded, targeted communications or instructions steering prescribers to the patented method. The door remains open if a complaint alleges concrete promotional acts aimed at the patented use, but this one, as framed, does not.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right that Grokster permits intent to be inferred circumstantially and that a skinny label is not categorical immunity, but their “constellation” approach still must plausibly allege the kind of purposeful, culpable encouragement Global-Tech and Commil require—affirmative steps directed to the patented method. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, where the pleaded facts are equally consistent with Congress’s § 355(j) section viii carve-out operating as intended and routine FDA-compliant marketing, the inference of specific intent is not plausible at Rule 12 without particularized allegations of directed communications or instructions steering prescribers to the patented use. Justice Jackson’s access-to-discovery concern is real, yet we cannot relax “actively induces” into foreseeability-plus in a way that destabilizes Hatch-Waxman reliance interests and effectively rewrites § 271(b). On this record, dismissal on the pleadings is appropriate while making clear that concrete, targeted promotion tied to the patented method would state a claim even with a skinny label.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are correct that Global-Tech and Grokster permit intent to be inferred from “expression and conduct,” and that a skinny label is not categorical immunity. But Chief Justice Roberts’s point remains decisive for me: the complaint must plausibly allege “active” inducement—affirmative steps purposefully directed to the patented method—rather than a “constellation” of facts that is equally consistent with FDA-compliant participation in Congress’s § viii carve-out plus foreseeable off-label prescribing. Under a textualist reading of § 271(b) as construed in Global-Tech and Commil, collapsing that requirement into foreseeability-plus would dilute “actively induces” and destabilize Hatch-Waxman’s reliance interests without a clear statutory basis. I therefore stay with Petitioner while emphasizing, as Roberts does, that targeted promotional acts tied to the patented use can still support inducement notwithstanding a skinny label.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability concern—that a “constellation” theory could degenerate into foreseeability and effectively nullify Congress’s § viii carve-out—squarely targets the weakest point of my position, and it rightly cautions us against treating predictable off-label use as “active” inducement under Global-Tech and Commil. But that critique does not justify, as Justice Alito suggests, a pleading-stage demand for a “clear, directed communication” that would operate as an extra-textual safe harbor whenever a skinny label exists, even though Grokster allows intent to be inferred from “expression and conduct” and discovery often supplies the context for intent. The workable line, consistent with procedural fairness, is that a skinny label is strong evidence against intent, yet not categorical immunity where the complaint plausibly alleges affirmative steps plausibly steering the market toward the patented method—something more than FDA-compliant participation plus market realities. On that understanding, I remain with Respondent because the statute focuses on the defendant’s purposeful encouragement, and we should not harden Rule 12 into a gatekeeping mechanism that forecloses circumstantial inducement claims before intent-revealing facts can be developed.

John Roberts.reasoning: Inducement under 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) requires well-pleaded facts plausibly showing "purposeful, culpable" encouragement and specific intent to bring about the patented use, not mere foreseeability that some physicians may prescribe off-label. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. and Commil confirm that knowledge and intent are essential elements, and Grokster underscores that ordinary distribution of a lawful product—especially one marketed pursuant to Congress’s Hatch-Waxman § 355(j) carve-out/skinny-label pathway—cannot alone supply inducement absent affirmative acts directed to infringement. Allowing inducement to proceed based on allegations consistent with lawful generic marketing risks expanding method-of-use patents beyond their proper scope and undermines the statutory balance and institutional reliance interests created by the skinny-label regime. A narrow ruling requiring more particularized allegations of intent and directed encouragement at the pleading stage best preserves precedent and the Hatch-Waxman framework while leaving room for liability on stronger, fact-specific proof.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who “actively induces infringement,” a textual requirement that demands purposeful, culpable conduct aimed at bringing about the patented method—not mere foreseeability that others might prescribe off-label or ordinary acts incident to lawful product distribution under Hatch-Waxman. Under Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., inducement requires knowledge and specific intent to cause infringement (or willful blindness), and Grokster likewise warns against theories that would compromise legitimate commerce absent “purposeful, culpable expression and conduct.” Where a generic has taken Congress’s authorized “carve-out/skinny label” path and the complaint rests on market realities and residual references consistent with noninfringing sales, the pleadings do not plausibly allege the affirmative encouragement of the patented use that § 271(b) demands. Allowing inducement liability on such allegations would effectively expand method-of-use patents beyond their statutory scope and undermine the limited pathway Congress created in 21 U.S.C. § 355(j).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who “actively induces” infringement, and this Court has read that adverb to require “affirmative steps to bring about the desired result,” not merely selling a lawful product into a market where infringement is foreseeable. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., 563 U.S. 754, 760, 766 (2011). Within the Hatch-Waxman framework, Congress specifically authorized section viii carve-outs to permit generic entry for non-patented uses (21 U.S.C. § 355(j)), and allowing inducement to proceed on a complaint grounded largely in market realities and ordinary FDA-compliant labeling/marketing risks collapsing that statutory pathway and effectively expanding method-of-use patents beyond their proper scope. At the pleading stage, I would require well-pleaded facts plausibly alleging a clear, targeted, affirmative act instructing or encouraging the patented method—consistent with Global-Tech and the Federal Circuit’s specific-intent requirement—rather than residual references and general promotion consistent with lawful competition.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 271(b) reaches affirmative acts taken with the intent to bring about infringement, and at the pleading stage the question is whether the complaint plausibly alleges that the generic’s labeling and marketing context amounted to encouragement of the patented method, not merely lawful sale of an FDA-approved product. Under Global-Tech, inducement requires knowledge and specific intent, but intent may be inferred from circumstantial facts—including how a product is positioned and communicated to prescribers and the market—so long as the allegations go beyond foreseeability of off-label use. The Hatch-Waxman “section viii” carve-out (21 U.S.C. § 355(j)(2)(A)(viii)) cannot operate as a categorical immunity where the pleaded facts suggest the carve-out was paired with communications or labeling choices that, in practical effect, steered use toward the patented indication; that is consistent with the Federal Circuit’s recognition in GSK v. Teva that a skinny label does not foreclose inducement when the overall conduct encourages the claimed method. Given the fact-intensive nature of inducement and the need to preserve access to remedies where wrongful conduct plausibly targets patented uses, dismissal at the threshold is unwarranted on these allegations.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only for “active” inducement, requiring knowledge and specific intent to bring about infringement, not mere foreseeability. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., 563 U.S. 754 (2011), and Grokster emphasize that intent may be inferred from purposeful, culpable expression and conduct—such as advertising or instructions—when the pleaded facts plausibly show the defendant encouraged the infringing use. In the Hatch-Waxman context, a skinny label under 21 U.S.C. § 355(j) reflects Congress’s carve-out pathway, but it does not categorically immunize a generic whose overall labeling/marketing communications, in context, plausibly cross the line into affirmatively promoting the patented method; at the pleading stage, a fact-specific “constellation” of such allegations can satisfy plausibility for intent and affirmative acts. Preserving the carve-out’s workability while allowing well-pleaded inducement claims to proceed best fits statutory coherence: it prevents method-of-use patents from becoming de facto product monopolies while still enforcing § 271(b) against purposeful encouragement of patented uses.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who "actively induces" infringement, and this Court has read that text to require "affirmative steps to bring about" the infringing act coupled with the requisite knowledge/intent. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., 563 U.S. 754, 760, 766 (2011). In the Hatch-Waxman setting, a § viii carve-out (a skinny label) is Congress’s textual mechanism for permitting lawful generic entry for nonpatented indications, and allowing inducement to rest on market realities or foreseeable off-label use—absent clear, specific promotional conduct directed to the patented method—risks converting lawful competition into liability contrary to § 271(b)’s “actively” requirement. At the pleading stage, allegations consistent with ordinary FDA-compliant selling of a lawfully labeled product are not enough under Global-Tech and Grokster’s insistence on “clear expression or other affirmative steps” fostering infringement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only for “active inducement,” which this Court has construed to require knowledge and specific intent to bring about infringement, not mere foreseeability or ordinary lawful sales. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. and Commil confirm that inducement is a purposeful-encouragement doctrine, and Grokster likewise requires “purposeful, culpable expression and conduct” directed to infringement; that standard counsels caution where the alleged acts largely track Congress’s Hatch-Waxman skinny-label pathway (21 U.S.C. § 355(j)) for marketing non-patented uses. In light of that statutory framework and the need for a workable, predictable rule that preserves Congress’s carve-out mechanism, I would require well-pleaded, nonconclusory facts showing affirmative acts aimed at the patented method—not allegations equally consistent with lawful competition under a section viii carve-out. The Federal Circuit’s more permissive, fact-constellation approach risks expanding § 271(b) beyond its traditional, intent-focused limits and undermining the skinny-label regime Congress authorized.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only for “active” inducement—purposeful, culpable conduct undertaken with knowledge and specific intent to bring about infringement, not mere foreseeability that infringement may occur. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. and Commil require well-pleaded facts supporting that intent and knowledge; allegations equally consistent with lawful conduct Congress authorized under Hatch-Waxman’s § 355(j) carve-out mechanism (a “skinny label”) do not plausibly establish inducement at the pleading stage. Where the generic’s label omits the patented indication and the remaining conduct is indistinguishable from ordinary marketing of an FDA-approved generic, allowing the claim to proceed risks converting § 271(b) into a negligence/foreseeability standard and undermines the statutory scheme’s text and structure. The complaint must plead affirmative acts directed to the patented method-of-use, not simply “market realities” or residual references consistent with noninfringing sales.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 271(b) requires purposeful, knowing encouragement of infringement, not mere foreseeability, but at the pleading stage a complaint need only plausibly allege specific intent and affirmative acts in context. Under Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. and Grokster, inducement turns on “purposeful, culpable” conduct, and a “skinny label” under the Hatch-Waxman framework (21 U.S.C. § 355(j)) does not categorically foreclose liability if the manufacturer’s overall labeling/marketing and marketplace positioning plausibly encouraged the patented method-of-use. Given the alleged fact-specific constellation suggesting active promotion despite the carve-out, allowing the claim to proceed advances procedural fairness by permitting discovery on intent and practical consequences without converting § 271(b) into strict liability. This approach also aligns with the Federal Circuit’s recognition in cases like GSK v. Teva and AstraZeneca v. Apotex that skinny-label inducement is a context-dependent inquiry rather than a per se safe harbor.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, based on the specific facts alleged, a generic drug manufacturer can be held liable for inducing infringement of a brand manufacturer’s method-of-use patents when the generic launches with a “skinny label” but other conduct allegedly encourages the patented use.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) (induced infringement), in the Hatch-Waxman context (including labeling/carve-outs under 21 U.S.C. § 355(j) and related FDA regulations).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Hikma) argue that the Federal Circuit improperly allowed an inducement claim to proceed based on an asserted “constellation of facts” that, in substance, treats FDA-approved generic marketing with a carved-out (skinny) label as actionable encouragement of infringement. They contend inducement requires specific intent and affirmative acts encouraging the patented use, and that allowing liability on attenuated inferences (e.g., the product’s existence on the market, legally compliant labeling, and ordinary distribution/reimbursement dynamics) undermines the Hatch-Waxman skinny-label pathway Congress created to permit generic entry for non-patented uses. Petitioners and supporting amici emphasize that expanding inducement theories here will chill carve-outs, delay generic launches, and increase drug costs, while creating uncertainty about what generic manufacturers may lawfully say or do when marketing an FDA-approved product for non-patented indications.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Amarin and related entities) argue that the complaint plausibly alleges inducement under § 271(b) because Hikma’s overall conduct—beyond merely selling a generic with a carved-out label—affirmatively encouraged or caused physicians and others to practice the patented method. They maintain that the Federal Circuit’s decision is fact-bound and correctly applies the pleading standard: the complaint alleges a particular combination of communications, product/labeling context, and market realities from which a reasonable inference of specific intent and encouragement of the patented use can be drawn. Respondents also contend that Hatch-Waxman does not immunize generics from inducement when their actions, taken as a whole, promote the patented indication notwithstanding a skinny label.
key_precedents: Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. (2011)
DSU Medical Corp. v. JMS Co. (Fed. Cir. 2006) (en banc in relevant part)
Warner-Lambert Co. v. Apotex Corp. (Fed. Cir. 2003)
AstraZeneca LP v. Apotex, Inc. (Fed. Cir. 2010)
Takeda Pharmaceuticals U.S.A., Inc. v. West-Ward Pharmaceutical Corp. (Fed. Cir. 2015)
GlaxoSmithKline LLC v. Teva Pharmaceuticals USA, Inc. (Fed. Cir. 2021)
Caraco Pharmaceutical Laboratories, Ltd. v. Novo Nordisk A/S (2012)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “constellation of facts” argument most directly tests my view, because inducement intent is often proven circumstantially and § 355(j) is not an immunity. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas emphasize, Global-Tech and DSU Medical require plausible allegations of the defendant’s own affirmative, purposefully directed encouragement of the patented use; otherwise intent collapses into mere foreseeability from lawful skinny-label marketing plus downstream prescribing and reimbursement practices. Caraco matters here because it confirms Congress expected a functioning section viii pathway, and an amorphous market-dynamics theory at the pleading stage risks making that pathway practically unworkable without clearer textual warrant in “actively induces.” I would therefore hold narrowly that these pleaded facts—regulatory compliance and predictable third-party conduct—do not plausibly allege the specific, directed encouragement § 271(b) demands, while leaving open liability where plaintiffs plead concrete promotional acts or instructions aimed at the carved-out use.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “constellation of facts” theory is the strongest response because inducement is often proven circumstantially, and § 355(j) does not by itself create an immunity. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 271(b)’s text—“actively induces”—and Global-Tech/DSU Medical require plausibly alleged affirmative, purposeful encouragement by the defendant itself, not liability derived primarily from foreseeable downstream prescribing and reimbursement behavior by third parties following an FDA-authorized skinny-label launch. Caraco underscores that Congress affirmatively preserved the section viii pathway, so we should not treat regulatory compliance plus market dynamics as a substitute for the “active” inducement element absent concrete, defendant-authored communications or conduct targeted to the patented use. Under Iqbal, nonconclusory allegations must make that directed encouragement plausible, and these pleadings do not.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that a “constellation of facts” can plausibly plead intent and affirmative conduct even with a skinny label—does not, as alleged here, satisfy § 271(b)’s textual requirement that the defendant “actively induces,” as construed in Global-Tech and DSU Medical to demand purposeful, affirmative steps directed to the infringing use. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that § 355(j) is not an inducement immunity, but that observation cannot erase the independent need for defendant-authored encouragement rather than liability driven by foreseeable downstream prescribing and reimbursement practices. Caraco matters because it confirms Congress expected lawful section viii launches; treating FDA-compliant labeling plus ordinary distribution and market dynamics as “active” inducement would, in practical effect, chill the carve-out pathway without clearer statutory warrant. If respondents had pleaded concrete promotional communications or instructions steering providers to the patented method, I would view the case differently, but on these pleadings Iqbal plausibility is not met.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s concern seriously that § 271(b) cannot be allowed to swallow Hatch–Waxman’s § 355(j) carve-out by treating foreseeability and lawful skinny-label sales as enough. But Global-Tech and DSU Medical do not require “magic words” of promotion; they require affirmative steps and specific intent, which can be plausibly inferred from non-label conduct when, in context, a defendant allegedly chooses communications, distribution, or reimbursement-facing actions that predictably steer prescribers toward the patented method. Caraco protects the availability of section viii as a regulatory pathway, not immunity from fact-bound inducement where the complaint alleges the generic exploited the pathway to encourage infringing use through its own conduct beyond mere compliance. At the Iqbal stage, the question is plausibility, and I would allow discovery to test whether the alleged conduct reflects purposeful encouragement versus mere downstream market dynamics.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that § 355(j)’s section viii pathway is not an inducement immunity and that intent can be inferred from circumstantial evidence, including conduct beyond the label. But under Global-Tech and DSU Medical, the inference must be tethered to the defendant’s own “active” encouragement—affirmative steps taken with the purpose of bringing about the patented use—not merely to foreseeable infringement produced by downstream prescribers, substitution rules, or reimbursement incentives. As Chief Justice Roberts argues, this is an administrable, text-grounded line that preserves inducement claims when plaintiffs plead concrete, defendant-authored promotion or instruction for the carved-out indication, while avoiding an interpretation that would effectively destabilize the Caraco-recognized section viii carve-out. On these pleadings, treating ordinary regulatory compliance plus market dynamics as the inducement “act” is too untethered from § 271(b)’s text and would make statutory coherence in Hatch–Waxman unworkable.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that § 355(j)’s section viii pathway is not an inducement “immunity,” and that intent can be inferred circumstantially; but her “constellation of facts” approach risks untethering the inference from § 271(b)’s textual requirement that the defendant “actively induces” infringement. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Global-Tech and DSU Medical demand affirmative, purposeful encouragement by the defendant, and allegations centered on FDA-compliant skinny labeling plus predictable third-party prescribing/reimbursement dynamics collapse specific intent into mere foreseeability. Caraco reinforces that Congress affirmatively designed a carve-out mechanism for nonpatented uses, and we should not effectively nullify it by allowing ordinary, lawful market participation to serve as the inducement act at the pleading stage absent concrete, defendant-authored communications or conduct directed to the patented method. On these pleadings, Iqbal plausibility is not satisfied, while leaving open liability where plaintiffs can allege targeted promotional steps aimed at the carved-out use.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “constellation of facts” argument most directly tests my view because inducement can be proven circumstantially and § 355(j) is not an immunity. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Global-Tech and DSU Medical require plausible allegations of the defendant’s own affirmative, purposeful encouragement of the patented method; treating FDA-compliant skinny-label marketing plus predictable substitution/reimbursement dynamics as the “affirmative step” collapses intent into foreseeability. Institutionally and as a matter of statutory coherence, Caraco’s recognition of the § viii pathway counsels a narrow, administrable line that preserves inducement liability where there are concrete, defendant-directed promotional acts, while rejecting pleadings that rely primarily on lawful regulatory compliance and third-party conduct. On these pleadings, I do not see a sufficiently specific, nonconclusory allegation tying the generic’s own conduct to encouragement of the carved-out use.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that § 355(j) creates no inducement immunity and that intent may be inferred circumstantially from a “constellation of facts,” even at the pleading stage. But under the text of § 271(b) (“actively induces”) as construed in Global-Tech and DSU Medical, Iqbal plausibility must be tied to the defendant’s own affirmative, purpose-driven encouragement of the patented method, not primarily to predictable third-party prescribing and reimbursement dynamics that follow a lawful section viii launch. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower framing is persuasive: we can reject these pleadings as insufficient while preserving inducement claims where plaintiffs allege concrete, defendant-authored promotional acts or instructions steering providers toward the carved-out use. Caraco’s recognition of Congress’s carve-out pathway reinforces the need for that limiting principle, because otherwise foreseeability plus regulatory compliance would effectively nullify an express statutory mechanism without clearer textual warrant.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that § 355(j)’s carve-out is not an inducement “immunity,” and that intent can be inferred circumstantially from a constellation of facts. But under Global-Tech and DSU Medical, that inference still must be tethered to the defendant’s own affirmative, purposive steps that actually encourage the patented method—not merely knowledge plus FDA-compliant skinny labeling and foreseeable downstream prescribing/reimbursement behavior by third parties. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, allowing ordinary Hatch–Waxman compliance and market realities to supply plausibility would, as a practical matter, destabilize the section viii pathway Congress preserved in Caraco and chill generic entry at the pleading stage. Procedural fairness and administrability therefore counsel requiring nonconclusory allegations of targeted promotion or other culpable, defendant-authored communications directed to the carved-out use before allowing discovery to proceed.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section viii of Hatch–Waxman, 21 U.S.C. § 355(j), reflects Congress’s deliberate choice to permit generic entry for unpatented uses via a “skinny label,” and we should be cautious about inducement theories under 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) that would, in practical effect, nullify that pathway. Inducement requires affirmative acts and specific intent to bring about infringement, not liability resting largely on market dynamics and legally compliant labeling; Global-Tech and DSU Medical emphasize that intent cannot be inferred from mere knowledge and lawful sales alone. Given the institutional costs of an expansive, fact-constellation approach that would chill carve-outs and disrupt the Hatch–Waxman balance, I would resolve this case narrowly by holding that the allegations as pleaded do not plausibly show the requisite purposeful encouragement of the patented method beyond what the statute and FDA regime already require. That approach preserves the narrow carve-out mechanism recognized in Caraco while leaving room for inducement liability where a generic’s own statements or conduct specifically promote the patented use.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) imposes liability only on one who "actively induces" infringement, which this Court has read to require "affirmative steps" taken with the purpose of bringing about infringement, not merely lawful, neutral conduct and market effects. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., 563 U.S. 754, 760, 768 n.8 (2011). In the Hatch-Waxman scheme, Congress specifically authorized carve-outs via § 355(j) to permit generic entry for non-patented uses; allowing an inducement claim to rest on a "constellation" of compliant skinny-label launch plus ordinary distribution/reimbursement dynamics would effectively nullify that statutory pathway without a clear textual basis. At the pleading stage, Iqbal requires plausible allegations of specific, culpable encouragement directed to the patented use; allegations that amount to inference from lawful sale and FDA-approved labeling do not plausibly satisfy § 271(b)'s active-inducement requirement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who “actively induces infringement,” which this Court has read to require affirmative steps and specific intent that infringement occur, not liability based on lawful market participation and attenuated inferences. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. holds that inducement demands knowledge (or willful blindness) and “affirmative steps to bring about the desired result,” and allowing a “constellation of facts” theory that effectively treats an FDA-compliant skinny label and ordinary distribution/reimbursement dynamics as encouragement risks collapsing § 271(b) into strict liability. In the Hatch-Waxman framework, Congress expressly created the section viii carve-out pathway (21 U.S.C. § 355(j)) to permit generic entry for non-patented uses, and construing § 271(b) to expose generics to inducement claims absent clear, targeted promotional acts would predictably chill that pathway and delay lower-cost drugs. On these allegations, the better reading is that respondents have not plausibly pleaded the kind of deliberate, affirmative encouragement required by § 271(b) as interpreted in Global-Tech and consistent with DSU Medical’s specific-intent requirement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 271(b) reaches a defendant who, with the requisite intent, takes affirmative steps to bring about infringement, and the question at the pleading stage is whether the alleged “constellation of facts” plausibly supports that inference. Under Global-Tech, inducement can be inferred where the complaint alleges knowledge (or willful blindness) of the patented method and conduct aimed at encouraging that use, and Hatch-Waxman’s § 355(j) “section viii” carve-out does not create an immunity if a generic’s non-label conduct effectively promotes the patented indication. Caraco confirms Congress wanted one patented use not to foreclose generic entry for nonpatented uses, but it does not foreclose fact-bound inducement claims when the generic allegedly steers the market toward the patented method despite a skinny label. Given the real-world risk that sophisticated marketing and distribution practices can drive prescribing that harms the patentee and distorts the statutory balance, I would allow the claim to proceed past the plausibility threshold.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 271(b) requires “affirmative acts” taken with “specific intent” to bring about infringement, not merely lawful marketing of an FDA-approved generic plus inferences drawn from ordinary reimbursement and prescribing dynamics. Reading the Hatch-Waxman Section viii carve-out (21 U.S.C. § 355(j)) as permitting approval and launch for non‑patented uses would be seriously undermined if a compliant “skinny label” can nonetheless yield inducement liability based on a broad “constellation” theory untethered to concrete promotional encouragement, contrary to the statutory design emphasized in Caraco. At the pleading stage, allegations must plausibly connect the defendant’s own communications or conduct to encouragement of the patented method; otherwise § 271(b) becomes an end-run around Section viii and creates an unworkable regime for generic entry. Global-Tech and DSU Medical supply the intent-and-affirmative-act guardrails that keep § 271(b) coherent with Hatch-Waxman’s carve-out pathway.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who “actively induces,” language that, by its plain meaning, requires affirmative steps taken with specific intent to bring about infringement, not merely lawful sale of a product capable of infringing uses. Global-Tech holds inducement demands “affirmative steps” and knowledge (at least willful blindness) that the encouraged acts constitute infringement; allegations resting on ordinary market dynamics and FDA-compliant labeling risk collapsing intent into foreseeability. In the Hatch-Waxman setting, Congress expressly authorized section viii carve-outs to permit generic entry for non-patented uses, see Caraco, and courts should be wary of converting that lawful pathway into a de facto presumption of inducement based on an amorphous “constellation of facts.” At the pleading stage under Iqbal, the complaint must plausibly allege purposeful, directed encouragement of the patented method—not just distribution and compliance with FDA labeling requirements for non-patented indications.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 271(b) requires “active” inducement—affirmative acts and specific intent to cause infringement—not merely placing a product on the market that has lawful, noninfringing uses. Global-Tech and DSU Medical demand knowledge and purposeful encouragement, and Caraco underscores that Hatch-Waxman’s § 355(j)(2)(A)(viii) carve-out is designed so “one patented use will not foreclose” generic marketing for unpatented uses, a mechanism that would be undermined if ordinary, FDA-compliant skinny-label marketing plus market dynamics sufficed. At the pleading stage, allowing a “constellation of facts” theory that effectively treats lawful carve-out labeling and standard distribution/reimbursement realities as inducement risks collapsing the § viii pathway Congress created and invites unworkable, legitimacy-damaging uncertainty for generic entry. Absent concrete alleged statements or conduct that expressly promotes the carved-out patented method, the complaint does not plausibly allege the requisite specific intent and affirmative encouragement under § 271(b).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only when a defendant "actively induces" infringement—text that, in its ordinary meaning, requires affirmative steps taken with the purpose of bringing about the infringing acts, not mere foreseeability that infringement will occur. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. holds inducement requires knowledge of the patent and that the induced acts constitute infringement, and it rejects treating inducement as a negligence-like foreseeability standard. In the Hatch-Waxman scheme, Congress expressly authorized generic entry via labeling carve-outs (21 U.S.C. § 355(j)), and the complaint’s reliance on legally compliant skinny-label marketing plus downstream market dynamics risks converting that authorized conduct into “active” encouragement without the clear, purposeful conduct Global-Tech and Grokster require. Given that induced infringement must be grounded in concrete allegations of targeted promotional acts evidencing specific intent, the pleaded “constellation of facts” is too attenuated to state a plausible § 271(b) claim.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Inducement under 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) requires purposeful, affirmative encouragement with knowledge of the patent and intent to cause the infringing acts, not mere foreseeability or market dynamics. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. and DSU Medical make clear that specific intent is an element, and a legally authorized Hatch-Waxman “skinny label” pathway under 21 U.S.C. § 355(j) should not be treated, without more concrete allegations of targeted promotion, as actionable encouragement of the carved-out patented use. At the pleading stage, allowing liability based on a generalized “constellation of facts” that substantially consists of compliant labeling plus ordinary distribution/reimbursement realities risks undermining Congress’s carve-out scheme (cf. Caraco) and chilling generic entry with predictable cost consequences. Procedural fairness favors requiring plaintiffs to plead nonconclusory facts showing the generic’s own culpable communications or conduct directed to the patented indication, rather than inferring intent from regulatory compliance and third-party behavior.
